case: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He has hypertension and has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 50 years. He has no abdominal or back pain. Pulse is 74/min, and blood pressure is 152/88 mm Hg (normal below 120/80 mm Hg). Physical examination shows a nontender, pulsatile mass just above the umbilicus. Ultrasonography shows fusiform dilation of the abdominal aorta below the renal arteries, with an outer diameter of 5.8 cm (normal about 2 cm). The renal arteries arise from normal-caliber aorta above the dilation. The diagnosis is infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).

questions.stem: He undergoes open surgical repair. During the operation, an unpaired artery arising from the anterior wall of the aneurysm at about the level of the third lumbar vertebra is ligated. If collateral flow to this artery's territory is poor, which of the following segments of bowel is at greatest risk for ischemia after surgery?
options: Sigmoid colon
Jejunum
Ascending colon
Second part of the duodenum
approach: Name the vessel: an unpaired anterior branch of the aorta at L3, below the renal arteries, is the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).
Recall the IMA territory: distal transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum.
Pick the segment in that territory that is classically injured after aortic repair: the sigmoid colon.
questions.why: The inferior mesenteric artery leaves the front of the aorta at about L3, so it arises from the segment that an infrarenal AAA usually involves. It supplies the left colon, including the sigmoid colon and upper rectum. When it is tied off during repair, the left colon depends on collaterals from the superior mesenteric artery (through the marginal artery) and from the internal iliac arteries. If these are poor, ischemic colitis develops, most often in the sigmoid colon.
whyNot: Correct.
The jejunum is supplied by jejunal branches of the superior mesenteric artery, which arises at about L1, above the renal arteries and above this aneurysm.
The ascending colon is supplied by the ileocolic and right colic branches of the superior mesenteric artery, which are not tied off in an infrarenal repair.
The second part of the duodenum is supplied by the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, from the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery.

topics: Branches of the abdominal aorta by vertebral level

questions.stem: Which of the following processes best explains the progressive weakening of the aortic wall in this patient's aneurysm?
options: Obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum
An intimal tear that lets blood split the media
Protease breakdown of medial elastin and collagen
Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells in the media
approach: Identify the setting: an older male smoker with hypertension and an infrarenal aneurysm has the typical atherosclerosis-associated AAA.
Recall what thins the media in AAA: inflammatory cells release matrix metalloproteinases that digest elastin and collagen.
Rule out mechanisms that belong to other aortic diseases (syphilis, dissection, arteritis).
questions.why: Typical AAAs arise in older smokers with atherosclerosis. Macrophages and other inflammatory cells in the aortic wall release matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that break down elastin and collagen in the media, and their inhibitors are reduced. Thick intimal plaque also slows diffusion of nutrients to the inner media. The thinned, weakened wall slowly dilates under arterial pressure.
whyNot: This describes tertiary syphilis, which narrows the vasa vasorum and causes aneurysms of the ascending aorta and arch, not the infrarenal aorta.
An intimal tear with blood tracking through the media describes aortic dissection, which is a different disease from a fusiform aneurysm.
Correct.
Granulomas with giant cells describe giant cell arteritis or Takayasu arteritis, which mainly involve the thoracic aorta and its branches.

topics: Matrix metalloproteinases in vessel wall remodeling

questions.stem: For a cylindrical vessel, Laplace's law states that wall tension equals transmural pressure times radius. If the pressure inside this patient's aneurysm equals that in a normal 2-cm aorta, which of the following is closest to the ratio of wall tension in the aneurysm to normal wall tension?
options: About 1.7 times
About 3 times
About 8 times
About 70 times
approach: Write Laplace's law for a cylinder: tension = pressure x radius.
Compare radii: 5.8 cm divided by 2 cm is 2.9, so the radius is about 3 times normal.
With pressure unchanged, tension rises in direct proportion to radius: about 3 times.
questions.why: Laplace's law for a cylinder says wall tension equals pressure times radius. The aneurysm's radius is about 2.9 times normal, so at the same pressure the wall tension is about 3 times normal. Because the aneurysm wall is also thinner, the stress on each unit of wall (tension divided by thickness) rises even more. This growing load on a weakening wall is why rupture risk climbs steeply as an aneurysm enlarges, and why elective repair is advised at about 5.5 cm in men.
whyNot: About 1.7 times would come from taking the square root of the radius ratio, which has no basis in Laplace's law.
Correct.
About 8 times comes from squaring the radius ratio, which would apply to cross-sectional area, not wall tension.
About 70 times comes from raising the radius ratio to the fourth power, which belongs to Poiseuille's law for resistance and flow.

questions.stem: Before the repair is scheduled, he develops fever and new back pain. One week earlier he had diarrhea after eating undercooked chicken. Temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F). Blood cultures grow a motile, oxidase-negative, gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose and produces hydrogen sulfide. CT scan shows rapid enlargement of the aneurysm with surrounding soft-tissue thickening. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?
options: Klebsiella pneumoniae
Shigella sonnei
Escherichia coli
Salmonella enterica
approach: List the lab clues: gram-negative rod, oxidase negative, motile, lactose nonfermenter, hydrogen sulfide producer.
Add the history: poultry-borne diarrhea followed by bacteremia in an older adult with a diseased aorta.
Match to the organism known for seeding atherosclerotic or aneurysmal arteries: nontyphoidal Salmonella.
questions.why: Nontyphoidal Salmonella is a motile, oxidase-negative, gram-negative rod that does not ferment lactose and makes hydrogen sulfide. It is commonly acquired from poultry and eggs. In adults over about 50, Salmonella bacteremia can seed atherosclerotic or aneurysmal arterial walls and cause an infected (mycotic) aneurysm, which tends to enlarge quickly and rupture.
whyNot: Klebsiella ferments lactose and is nonmotile, so it does not fit these culture results.
Shigella does not ferment lactose but is nonmotile and does not produce hydrogen sulfide. It has no animal reservoir and rarely enters the bloodstream.
Escherichia coli usually ferments lactose and does not produce hydrogen sulfide.
Correct.

dx: Acute Stanford type A aortic dissection in Marfan syndrome
case: A 34-year-old man with Marfan syndrome is brought to the emergency department because of sudden, severe, tearing chest pain that radiates to the area between his shoulder blades. He had bilateral ectopia lentis as a teenager. He is 196 cm tall. Blood pressure is 158/92 mm Hg in the right arm and 124/76 mm Hg in the left arm. Physical examination shows arachnodactyly. A soft early diastolic murmur is heard along the left sternal border. CT angiography shows an intimal flap that begins in the ascending aorta just above the aortic valve and extends beyond the origin of the left subclavian artery. The diagnosis is acute Stanford type A aortic dissection.

questions.stem: His Marfan syndrome is caused by a mutation in FBN1. Normal fibrillin-1 microfibrils sequester a growth factor in a latent form in the extracellular matrix. Increased signaling by which of the following factors contributes to degeneration of this patient's aortic media?
options: Platelet-derived growth factor
Tumor necrosis factor alpha
Transforming growth factor beta
Vascular endothelial growth factor
approach: Name the gene product: FBN1 encodes fibrillin-1, a scaffold for elastic fibers.
Recall the second role of fibrillin-1: it binds and sequesters latent TGF-beta in the matrix.
Connect the defect to disease: abnormal fibrillin releases too much active TGF-beta, which damages the aortic wall.
questions.why: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in FBN1 on chromosome 15. Fibrillin-1 forms microfibrils that support elastic fibers and also hold transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) in a latent complex. Mutant fibrillin fails to sequester TGF-beta, and the excess signaling contributes to loss of smooth muscle and elastic tissue in the aortic media. This medial weakness leads to aortic root dilation and dissection.
whyNot: Platelet-derived growth factor drives smooth muscle migration in atherosclerosis but is not stored by fibrillin-1.
Tumor necrosis factor alpha is an inflammatory cytokine, and Marfan aortic disease is characteristically noninflammatory.
Correct.
Vascular endothelial growth factor drives new vessel growth and is not held latent by fibrillin microfibrils.

questions.stem: The false lumen of an aortic dissection forms within the aortic wall, usually between the middle and outer thirds of one layer. In a normal adult aorta, which of the following best describes the main components of that layer?
options: Fenestrated elastic laminae with smooth muscle between them
Endothelium resting on a thin layer of loose connective tissue
Loose collagen containing vasa vasorum, nerves, and fibroblasts
Longitudinal smooth muscle bundles with few elastic fibers
approach: Identify the layer: a dissection plane runs within the tunica media.
Recall that the aorta is an elastic artery whose media is its thickest layer.
Describe that media: many concentric fenestrated elastic laminae with smooth muscle cells, collagen, and ground substance between them.
questions.why: In a dissection, blood enters through an intimal tear and splits the tunica media, most often between its middle and outer thirds. The aorta is an elastic artery. Its media is the thickest layer and contains dozens of concentric, fenestrated elastic laminae with smooth muscle cells, collagen, and proteoglycan ground substance between them. These laminae store energy during systole and recoil in diastole, and their loss is what makes the media vulnerable to splitting.
whyNot: Correct.
This describes the tunica intima. The intimal tear is the entry point, but the false lumen runs in the media.
This describes the tunica adventitia, the outer layer that carries vasa vasorum and nerves to the outer wall.
Longitudinal smooth muscle bundles are typical of the adventitia of large veins such as the inferior vena cava, not the aortic wall.

questions.stem: Two hours later, he becomes confused. Pulse is 128/min, and blood pressure is 84/60 mm Hg. Jugular venous distention is present, and heart sounds are muffled. Systolic pressure decreases by 18 mm Hg with each inspiration. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the decrease in systolic pressure during inspiration?
options: Inspiration lowers venous return to the right heart, reducing output
Lung expansion compresses the false lumen and narrows the true lumen
Inspiration raises vagal tone, slowing the heart and lowering output
Right ventricular filling rises and bows the septum to the left
approach: Recognize cardiac tamponade: hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds after a type A dissection ruptures into the pericardium.
Recall the effect of inspiration: lower intrathoracic pressure increases venous return to the right ventricle.
Apply the fixed pericardial volume: the right ventricle can only expand by bowing the septum left, so left ventricular filling and stroke volume fall.
questions.why: A type A dissection can rupture back into the pericardial sac, causing hemopericardium and tamponade. The tight pericardium fixes the total volume of the heart. During inspiration, falling intrathoracic pressure draws more blood into the right ventricle, which can only enlarge by pushing the interventricular septum into the left ventricle. Left ventricular filling and stroke volume fall, so systolic pressure drops by more than 10 mm Hg with inspiration (pulsus paradoxus). Pooling of blood in the expanding pulmonary veins adds to the fall.
whyNot: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart. It does not reduce it.
There is no recognized mechanism by which lung expansion compresses the false lumen to cause a cyclic fall in pressure.
Inspiration lowers vagal tone and slightly speeds the heart (sinus arrhythmia), the opposite of this option.
Correct.

topics: Effects of respiration on venous return

questions.stem: A resected segment of his ascending aorta is examined microscopically. Which of the following findings in the media is most characteristic of the process that predisposed him to dissection?
options: Granulomas with multinucleated giant cells throughout the media
Elastic fiber breakup, smooth muscle loss, and mucoid pools
Plasma cells around narrowed, thickened vasa vasorum
Fibrinoid necrosis with neutrophils across the vessel wall
approach: Identify the predisposing condition: Marfan syndrome weakens the aortic media.
Name the lesion: cystic medial degeneration.
Describe it: elastic fiber fragmentation, smooth muscle loss, and pools of proteoglycan-rich ground substance, with little inflammation.
questions.why: Marfan syndrome and long-standing hypertension both predispose to dissection through cystic medial degeneration. The media shows fragmented and separated elastic fibers, loss of smooth muscle cells, and small cleftlike or cystic spaces filled with proteoglycan-rich (mucoid) ground substance. Inflammation is characteristically absent. The weakened media splits easily once blood enters through an intimal tear.
whyNot: Granulomas with giant cells describe giant cell arteritis or Takayasu arteritis.
Correct.
Plasma cells around narrowed vasa vasorum describe syphilitic aortitis, which causes aneurysms of the ascending aorta but rarely dissection.
Fibrinoid necrosis with neutrophils describes necrotizing vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa, which affects medium-sized arteries.

dx: Atherosclerotic carotid artery disease with amaurosis fugax
case: A 66-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an episode of painless vision loss in her right eye yesterday. She describes a shade coming down over the eye that lasted about 5 minutes and then lifted. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension and smoked for 30 years. Blood pressure is 148/90 mm Hg (normal below 120/80 mm Hg). A bruit is heard over the right side of the neck near the angle of the mandible. Serum LDL cholesterol is 168 mg/dL (optimal below 100 mg/dL). Duplex ultrasonography shows an ulcerated plaque at the origin of the right internal carotid artery that narrows the lumen diameter by about 50%. The diagnosis is atherosclerotic carotid artery disease with amaurosis fugax, a warning sign of high stroke risk.

questions.stem: Her transient vision loss was most likely caused by a small embolus from the plaque that lodged in a branch of which of the following arteries?
options: Right posterior cerebral artery
Right ophthalmic artery
Left middle cerebral artery
Right superficial temporal artery
approach: Note that vision was lost in one eye only, which points to the retina rather than the visual cortex or optic radiations.
Trace the path: plaque at the right internal carotid origin, up the internal carotid, into its first major intracranial branch.
That branch is the ophthalmic artery, which gives off the central retinal artery.
questions.why: Monocular vision loss means the retina or optic nerve of that eye lost blood flow. The internal carotid artery has no branches in the neck. Its first major branch inside the skull is the ophthalmic artery, which gives off the central retinal artery. An embolus from an ulcerated plaque at the internal carotid origin can travel into this branch and cause transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax).
whyNot: The posterior cerebral artery supplies the occipital cortex. Its ischemia causes a homonymous hemianopia that affects the visual field of both eyes, and it usually arises from the basilar artery, not the carotid.
Correct.
The left middle cerebral artery cannot receive an embolus from a right carotid plaque, and middle cerebral territory loss affects both eyes' visual fields, not one eye.
The superficial temporal artery is a branch of the external carotid artery and does not supply the retina. It is the classic site of giant cell arteritis.

topics: Branches of the internal carotid artery

questions.stem: At the plaque, the lumen radius is about half of normal. If flow is laminar and blood viscosity and segment length are unchanged, the resistance of the narrowed segment has increased by approximately which of the following factors?
options: About 2 times
About 4 times
About 16 times
About 256 times
approach: Recall Poiseuille's law: resistance is proportional to viscosity times length divided by radius to the fourth power.
Halving the radius divides the denominator by 2 to the fourth power, which is 16.
So resistance in that segment rises about 16 times.
questions.why: Poiseuille's law states that resistance equals 8 times viscosity times length, divided by pi times the radius to the fourth power. Because radius is raised to the fourth power, halving the radius raises resistance 16 times. A 50% diameter narrowing is the same as halving the radius. This steep relationship explains why modest further plaque growth or a thrombus on an ulcerated plaque can sharply cut flow.
whyNot: About 2 times would be true only if resistance were inversely proportional to radius itself.
About 4 times would be true if resistance depended on radius squared (cross-sectional area).
Correct.
About 256 times is the increase when the radius falls to one quarter of normal (4 to the fourth power).

questions.stem: Macrophages in her plaque become foam cells by taking up oxidized LDL. Which of the following best explains why these cells continue to take up cholesterol after they are heavily loaded?
options: Scavenger receptors are not downregulated by cholesterol
LDL receptor numbers rise as the cell's cholesterol increases
HDL delivers extra stored cholesterol into macrophages
SREBP-2 is activated by high levels of cell cholesterol
approach: Identify the receptor: oxidized LDL enters macrophages through scavenger receptors such as SR-A and CD36.
Contrast with the LDL receptor, which is shut down by high intracellular cholesterol through SREBP-2.
Conclude that scavenger receptor uptake has no feedback brake, so lipid keeps accumulating.
questions.why: Oxidized LDL in the intima is recognized by macrophage scavenger receptors, such as SR-A and CD36, which are pattern recognition receptors of innate immunity. Unlike the LDL receptor, these receptors are not downregulated when the cell fills with cholesterol. Uptake continues, cholesteryl ester droplets build up, and the cell becomes a foam cell. Loaded macrophages also release cytokines that recruit more inflammatory cells.
whyNot: Correct.
LDL receptor expression falls when cell cholesterol rises, because SREBP-2 is held inactive. This feedback is the reason native LDL does not overload cells.
HDL removes cholesterol from macrophages (reverse cholesterol transport). It does not load them.
SREBP-2 is activated when cell cholesterol is low and suppressed when it is high.

questions.stem: Her plaque formed at the carotid bifurcation, a common site of atherosclerosis. Which of the following local conditions best explains why arterial branch points are prone to plaque formation?
options: High, steady laminar shear stress on endothelial cells
Lower pressure at branches that draws plasma lipids inward
Absent vasa vasorum causing ischemia of the inner wall
Low and oscillating shear stress on endothelial cells
approach: Recall where plaques form: branch points, ostia, and the outer wall of the carotid bulb.
Link flow pattern to endothelial behavior: steady laminar flow is protective, disturbed flow is not.
Choose low, oscillating shear stress, which turns on proinflammatory, adhesive endothelial genes.
questions.why: Steady laminar flow with high shear stress induces protective endothelial genes, including endothelial nitric oxide synthase, which keep the surface anti-inflammatory and less permeable. At branch points such as the carotid bulb, flow separates and recirculates, so shear stress is low and changes direction. Endothelium there makes less nitric oxide, expresses adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1, and lets more LDL into the intima. This is why plaques cluster at bifurcations and ostia.
whyNot: High, steady laminar shear stress protects the endothelium and is found in straight segments where plaques are less common.
Pressure differences between branches do not draw lipids into the wall. LDL entry depends on endothelial permeability.
The inner wall of all arteries is nourished by diffusion from the lumen, so lack of vasa vasorum there is not specific to branch points.
Correct.

dx: Atherosclerosis risk in metabolic syndrome with atherogenic dyslipidemia
case: A 48-year-old man is evaluated at a workplace health screening. He has a sedentary lifestyle and a diet high in fast food. Waist circumference is 108 cm (risk threshold above 102 cm in men). Blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg (normal below 120/80 mm Hg). Fasting laboratory studies show glucose 118 mg/dL (normal 70 to 99 mg/dL), triglycerides 260 mg/dL (normal below 150 mg/dL), HDL cholesterol 34 mg/dL (desired above 40 mg/dL in men), and LDL cholesterol 138 mg/dL (optimal below 100 mg/dL). High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) is 4.2 mg/L (low risk below 1.0 mg/L). Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 45 mg/g (normal below 30 mg/g). The diagnosis is metabolic syndrome with atherogenic dyslipidemia, which raises his risk of atherosclerosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's elevated fasting triglyceride concentration?
options: Loss of hepatic LDL receptors slowing the clearance of LDL
Reduced hepatic secretion of apoB-100 particles
Increased intestinal absorption of dietary cholesterol
Increased hepatic VLDL secretion from excess fatty acids
approach: Identify the driver: central obesity with high glucose points to insulin resistance.
Follow the fatty acids: insulin normally suppresses adipocyte lipolysis, so resistant fat cells release more free fatty acids to the liver.
The liver packages the extra fatty acids as triglyceride in VLDL, so fasting triglycerides rise.
questions.why: In insulin resistance, insulin fails to suppress hormone-sensitive lipase in adipocytes, so more free fatty acids flow to the liver. The liver re-esterifies them into triglyceride and secretes more VLDL with apoB-100. Reduced lipoprotein lipase activity slows VLDL clearance and adds to the rise. Through cholesteryl ester transfer protein, triglyceride then moves from VLDL into HDL and LDL, which explains his low HDL and the small, dense LDL typical of this pattern.
whyNot: Loss of LDL receptors raises LDL cholesterol, as in familial hypercholesterolemia, but does not by itself raise fasting triglycerides.
Reduced apoB-100 secretion would lower VLDL and triglycerides. Insulin resistance does the opposite.
Dietary cholesterol absorption mainly affects LDL cholesterol. Fasting triglycerides come from hepatic VLDL, not from chylomicrons.
Correct.

questions.stem: In a research study, infusion of acetylcholine into his brachial artery causes much less forearm vasodilation than in healthy controls. Infusion of sodium nitroprusside, which releases nitric oxide directly, causes a normal response. Which of the following steps is most likely impaired?
options: Smooth muscle guanylyl cyclase response to nitric oxide
Release of nitric oxide by the endothelium
Smooth muscle beta-2 receptor signaling through cAMP
Alpha-1 receptor signaling in forearm arterioles
approach: Recall the acetylcholine pathway: acetylcholine acts on endothelial muscarinic receptors to make nitric oxide.
Use the control: nitroprusside bypasses the endothelium and relaxes smooth muscle normally, so the smooth muscle response is intact.
Locate the defect in the endothelium: reduced release and availability of nitric oxide (endothelial dysfunction).
questions.why: Acetylcholine binds endothelial M3 receptors, raises endothelial calcium, and activates endothelial nitric oxide synthase. Nitric oxide diffuses into smooth muscle, activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, raises cGMP, and relaxes the vessel. Nitroprusside supplies nitric oxide without the endothelium, so a normal response to it proves the smooth muscle pathway works. A blunted acetylcholine response with a normal nitroprusside response is the standard test result for endothelial dysfunction, an early step in atherosclerosis that is common in insulin resistance.
whyNot: A smooth muscle guanylyl cyclase defect would also blunt the response to nitroprusside, which was normal.
Correct.
Beta-2 receptors respond to epinephrine, not acetylcholine, and a beta-2 defect would not explain this test result.
Alpha-1 receptors cause vasoconstriction. Acetylcholine-induced dilation does not depend on them.

questions.stem: Visceral adipose tissue in central obesity contains many activated macrophages. Which of the following cytokines released from this tissue most directly stimulates hepatic synthesis of C-reactive protein in this patient?
options: Interleukin 4
Interleukin 10
Interleukin 6
Interleukin 2
approach: Recognize CRP as an acute phase protein made by hepatocytes.
Recall the main cytokine that induces acute phase protein synthesis: interleukin 6.
Link visceral fat macrophages and adipocytes as an ongoing source of interleukin 6 in obesity.
questions.why: C-reactive protein is an acute phase protein made by hepatocytes. Interleukin 6 is the main signal that drives its synthesis, with help from interleukin 1 and tumor necrosis factor. In central obesity, activated macrophages and adipocytes in visceral fat release interleukin 6 steadily, producing low-grade chronic inflammation. An hs-CRP above about 3 mg/L marks higher cardiovascular risk.
whyNot: Interleukin 4 is a Th2 cytokine that drives IgE class switching and does not induce CRP.
Interleukin 10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that dampens acute phase responses.
Correct.
Interleukin 2 is a T-cell growth factor and does not drive hepatic acute phase protein synthesis.

questions.stem: Two years later, a kidney biopsy is performed because of increasing albuminuria. It shows small arterioles with walls thickened by homogeneous, glassy, eosinophilic material and narrowed lumens. Which of the following processes most likely produced this arteriolar change?
options: Plasma proteins leaking into the wall, plus excess matrix
Concentric smooth muscle growth with duplicated basement membrane
Calcium deposition in the media of muscular arteries
Lipid-laden macrophages collecting beneath the endothelium
approach: Name the lesion: glassy pink arteriolar wall thickening is hyaline arteriolosclerosis.
Link it to his conditions: chronic hypertension and diabetes or prediabetes.
Recall the mechanism: plasma protein leakage through injured endothelium plus extra matrix from smooth muscle cells.
questions.why: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis is a form of arteriosclerosis seen with long-standing hypertension, diabetes, and aging. Chronic hemodynamic and metabolic stress injures the endothelium, so plasma proteins leak into the arteriolar wall. Smooth muscle cells also lay down extra extracellular matrix. The result is homogeneous pink wall thickening that narrows the lumen and causes ischemic injury to the kidney (nephrosclerosis).
whyNot: Correct.
Concentric, onion-skin smooth muscle growth with duplicated basement membrane is hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis, seen in severe (malignant) hypertension.
Medial calcification is Monckeberg medial sclerosis, which affects muscular arteries rather than arterioles and does not narrow the lumen.
Lipid-laden macrophages beneath the endothelium form fatty streaks and atheromas in large and medium arteries, not arterioles.

case: A 31-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation after his father died of a myocardial infarction at age 46. He does not smoke and is not obese. Physical examination shows nodular thickening of both Achilles tendons and bilateral corneal arcus. Fasting serum LDL cholesterol is 292 mg/dL (optimal below 100 mg/dL), triglycerides are 120 mg/dL (normal below 150 mg/dL), and HDL cholesterol is 48 mg/dL (desired above 40 mg/dL in men). Thyroid and kidney function test results are normal. Genetic testing shows one pathogenic variant in the LDL receptor gene (LDLR). The diagnosis is heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia.

questions.stem: His wife also has heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia caused by a different pathogenic LDLR variant. Which of the following is the probability that their first child inherits a pathogenic variant from each parent and has the severe form of the disease?
approach: Recognize the inheritance: familial hypercholesterolemia is autosomal dominant, and having two pathogenic alleles causes a more severe disease.
Each heterozygous parent passes the variant to a child with a probability of 1/2.
Multiply: 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4, or 25%.
questions.why: Familial hypercholesterolemia is autosomal dominant with a gene dosage effect. Each heterozygous parent passes the pathogenic allele half the time, so the chance that a child inherits both is 1/2 x 1/2, or 25%. A child with two pathogenic alleles (homozygous or compound heterozygous) has very little LDL receptor function, LDL cholesterol often above 500 mg/dL, and coronary disease that can begin in childhood. Each child also has a 50% chance of being heterozygous and a 25% chance of being unaffected.
whyNot: Correct.
50% is the chance that a child is heterozygous, carrying exactly one pathogenic allele.
75% is the chance that a child has at least one pathogenic allele (affected in either form).
100% would apply only if a parent had two pathogenic alleles and could pass nothing else.

topics: Autosomal dominant inheritance with gene dosage

questions.stem: In his hepatocytes, fewer functional LDL receptors means less LDL-derived cholesterol reaches the cell interior. Which of the following best describes the hepatocyte response to the decreased intracellular cholesterol?
options: SREBP-2 stays in the ER, lowering HMG-CoA reductase
ACAT activity rises, storing more cholesteryl ester
HMG-CoA reductase is ubiquitinated and degraded faster
SREBP-2 is activated, increasing HMG-CoA reductase
approach: Identify the sensor: SCAP in the endoplasmic reticulum senses membrane cholesterol.
Low cholesterol lets SCAP carry SREBP-2 to the Golgi, where it is cleaved and released.
The released SREBP-2 enters the nucleus and raises transcription of HMG-CoA reductase and the LDL receptor.
questions.why: When cholesterol in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane is low, SCAP escorts SREBP-2 to the Golgi. Two proteases (S1P and S2P) cleave it, and the freed transcription factor enters the nucleus and binds sterol regulatory elements. This raises synthesis of HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, and of the LDL receptor. In heterozygotes, the normal allele is upregulated this way, which is why they respond to statins.
whyNot: SREBP-2 stays in the endoplasmic reticulum when cell cholesterol is high, not low.
ACAT esterifies cholesterol for storage when the cell has excess cholesterol. Low cholesterol reduces its activity.
Faster ubiquitination and degradation of HMG-CoA reductase is triggered by high sterol levels, not low ones.
Correct.

questions.stem: An elastic-stained section of his father's left anterior descending artery shows a plaque with foam cells and a lipid core. The plaque lies between the endothelium and a dark, wavy band, and beneath the band are layers of smooth muscle cells. Which of the following correctly identifies the layer containing the plaque and the band?
options: Media; the band is the external elastic lamina
Intima; the band is the internal elastic lamina
Adventitia; the band is the external elastic lamina
Media; the band is the internal elastic lamina
approach: Recall the layers of a muscular artery: intima, internal elastic lamina, media, external elastic lamina, adventitia.
Place the plaque: it sits between the endothelium and the first elastic band, so it is in the intima.
Identify the band: the elastic layer just under the intima, above the smooth muscle media, is the internal elastic lamina.
questions.why: Coronary arteries are muscular arteries. From the lumen outward they have an intima (endothelium and subendothelial connective tissue), a wavy internal elastic lamina, a media of circular smooth muscle, an external elastic lamina, and an adventitia. Atherosclerotic plaques form in the intima, above the internal elastic lamina. As a plaque grows, the internal elastic lamina can fragment and the underlying media thins.
whyNot: The external elastic lamina lies outside the media, so it cannot be the band directly beneath the plaque with smooth muscle below it.
Correct.
The adventitia is the outermost layer, and atheromas do not form there.
The media is the smooth muscle layer beneath the band. The plaque is above the band, so it is in the intima.

questions.stem: His father's fatal infarction most likely followed rupture of a coronary plaque with a thin fibrous cap. T-helper 1 cells in such plaques release a cytokine that decreases collagen synthesis by intimal smooth muscle cells and activates macrophages. Which of the following cytokines is most likely responsible?
options: Interleukin 5
Transforming growth factor beta
Interferon gamma
Interleukin 10
approach: Recognize the cell: T-helper 1 cells.
Recall their signature cytokine: interferon gamma, which activates macrophages.
Link it to cap thinning: interferon gamma lowers smooth muscle collagen production while activated macrophages release matrix metalloproteinases.
questions.why: The fibrous cap is made of collagen laid down by intimal smooth muscle cells. Th1 cells in the plaque release interferon gamma, which reduces smooth muscle collagen synthesis and activates macrophages. Activated macrophages release matrix metalloproteinases that digest the cap. A thin cap over a large lipid core is the typical vulnerable plaque that ruptures and triggers thrombosis and myocardial infarction.
whyNot: Interleukin 5 is a Th2 cytokine that drives eosinophil growth and does not reduce cap collagen.
Transforming growth factor beta stimulates collagen synthesis and tends to stabilize plaques.
Correct.
Interleukin 10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine that dampens macrophage activation.

dx: Peripheral arterial disease with intermittent claudication
case: A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician because of cramping pain in her right calf that begins after she walks about two blocks and resolves within a few minutes of standing still. She has smoked for 40 years. Physical examination shows normal femoral pulses bilaterally. The right popliteal, dorsalis pedis, and posterior tibial pulses are diminished. The skin of the right lower leg is shiny with sparse hair. Resting ankle-brachial index (ABI) is 0.62 on the right (normal 1.0 to 1.4) and 1.05 on the left. The diagnosis is peripheral arterial disease of the right leg with intermittent claudication.

questions.stem: Based on the pulse findings and the location of her pain, stenosis of which of the following arteries is most likely?
options: Common iliac artery
Deep artery of the thigh (profunda femoris)
Superficial femoral artery
Anterior tibial artery
approach: Use the pulses: a normal femoral pulse places the lesion below the common femoral artery, and a weak popliteal pulse places it above the popliteal artery.
The artery between those two points that continues to the popliteal is the superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal.
Confirm with symptoms: calf claudication fits a femoropopliteal lesion, one level above the painful muscles.
questions.why: The femoral artery continues down the thigh as the superficial femoral artery, passes through the adductor canal, and becomes the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus. A normal femoral pulse with a weak popliteal pulse localizes the narrowing to this segment. The superficial femoral artery in the adductor canal is the most common site of symptomatic atherosclerosis in the leg, and it typically causes calf claudication.
whyNot: A common iliac lesion would weaken the femoral pulse and usually causes buttock and thigh claudication.
The deep artery of the thigh supplies the thigh muscles and does not continue to the popliteal artery, so narrowing there would not weaken the popliteal pulse.
Correct.
The anterior tibial artery arises below the popliteal artery, so narrowing there would not weaken the popliteal pulse.

topics: Localizing PAD by pulses and symptoms

questions.stem: Her calf blood flow at rest is normal, yet pain develops with walking. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: Walking triggers sympathetic constriction of the calf arterioles
Arterioles offset the stenosis at rest but not during exercise
Exercise lowers arterial pressure, so less blood reaches the calf
Calf contraction collapses the stenosis and stops flow completely
approach: Think of the circuit as two resistances in series: the fixed stenosis and the adjustable arterioles downstream.
At rest, the arterioles dilate enough to keep total resistance and flow normal.
During exercise the arterioles are already dilated, so total resistance cannot fall enough, and flow cannot rise to meet demand.
questions.why: The stenosis adds a fixed resistance in series with the calf arterioles. At rest, the arterioles dilate to compensate, so resting flow stays normal. During walking, muscle metabolites call for flow several times higher, but the arterioles have little dilation left and the stenosis caps the flow. The pressure drop across the stenosis also grows as flow increases. Oxygen supply falls short of demand, anaerobic metabolites build up, and pain begins. It eases when demand drops with rest.
whyNot: During exercise, local metabolic vasodilation in working muscle overrides sympathetic constriction.
Correct.
Arterial systolic pressure rises during walking. It does not fall.
Muscle contraction does not close a proximal arterial stenosis. The problem is limited flow reserve, not complete collapse.

questions.stem: She drinks alcohol heavily and eats few vegetables. Fasting plasma homocysteine is 24 µmol/L (normal 5 to 15 µmol/L), mean corpuscular volume (MCV) is 106 fL (normal 80 to 100 fL), and serum methylmalonic acid is within the reference range. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins most likely explains her elevated homocysteine concentration?
options: Cobalamin (vitamin B12)
Pyridoxine (vitamin B6)
Thiamine (vitamin B1)
Folate (vitamin B9)
approach: Recall that homocysteine is remethylated to methionine by methionine synthase, which needs N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate and vitamin B12.
Use methylmalonic acid to separate the two: it rises in B12 deficiency and stays normal in folate deficiency.
Combine with the large red cells and poor diet with heavy drinking: folate deficiency.
questions.why: Methionine synthase moves a methyl group from N5-methyl-tetrahydrofolate, through methylcobalamin, to homocysteine to make methionine. A lack of folate or B12 therefore raises homocysteine and causes a macrocytic anemia. Only B12 deficiency also raises methylmalonic acid, because B12 is a cofactor for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. High homocysteine injures endothelium and promotes thrombosis, and it is a recognized risk factor for atherosclerosis.
whyNot: B12 deficiency would raise both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid. Her methylmalonic acid is normal.
B6 deficiency can raise homocysteine through cystathionine beta-synthase, but it causes a microcytic (sideroblastic) anemia, not a high MCV.
Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase and does not affect homocysteine metabolism.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following serious outcomes is she most likely to have over the next 5 years?
options: Myocardial infarction or stroke
Major amputation of the right leg
Rupture of an abdominal aortic aneurysm
Pulmonary embolism
approach: Recognize that PAD is a marker of widespread atherosclerosis.
Recall that most patients with claudication stay stable in the leg, and few need amputation.
Conclude that coronary and cerebrovascular events are the most common serious outcomes and the leading cause of death.
questions.why: Peripheral arterial disease reflects atherosclerosis throughout the arterial tree, so patients with it usually also have coronary and carotid disease. In people with claudication, myocardial infarction and stroke are far more common than limb loss and are the main causes of death. Only a small minority progress to critical limb ischemia or major amputation over five years. This is why PAD is treated as a coronary risk equivalent.
whyNot: Correct.
Major amputation occurs in only a small minority of patients with claudication over five years, and the risk is lower in those who stop smoking.
PAD raises the chance of having an AAA, but rupture is much less common than myocardial infarction or stroke in this group.
Pulmonary embolism arises from venous thrombosis and is not a typical consequence of arterial atherosclerosis.
